Chart system · Concept 03 · View 1 of 5, White

Instrument

Every chart here is a module with the same seven slots, in the same order, on the Signal Grid's 8 px rhythm. One generator per chart form draws each module at three widths, so a builder can make the next chart from the kit without asking. Atlas record numbers print as small index labels where they help a reader find the record, and texture or an open mark carries the second code after color, as the atlas's evidence lines do. The same module works as a still image and as a panel with a Chart and Table switch; the System view says which parts change.

  • NewsprintThe same ten modules on the warm ground, from the same generators.
  • CharcoalTwo modules on the dark ground, with the dark palette.
  • Social cardOne module set as a 1080 by 1350 card.
  • SystemThe kit on one sheet: slots, sizes, type, marks, codes, palettes and rules.

Each chart sits in its module. The tinted panel beside it is the studio's note for reviewers and is not chart copy.

Studio note, not chart copy

S01 · Big number in context

Reader question. Do Republicans and Democrats agree on anything about Congress?

Why this form. A big number answers yes at a glance; the party bars beside it show the two figures one point apart, and the votes show what Congress did three years later.

Kit. Drawn by big_number(). Column module, 866 px; artboards 866, 560 and 328 px.

Studio note, not chart copy

S02 · Line with event notes

Reader question. What happened to child poverty when the expanded child tax credit was paid, and after it lapsed?

Why this form. A line shows the fall to 2021 and the climb back; the official measure in Stone shows what the supplemental measure counts, and the breaks show where the Census Bureau changed its method.

Kit. Drawn by line_events(). Column module, 866 px; artboards 866, 560 and 328 px.

Studio note, not chart copy

S03 · Ranked bar

Reader question. Who changed the rules: voters, courts or legislatures?

Why this form. Seven instruments ranked by count answer who made the most changes; splitting each bar by the atlas's direction code shows which way each instrument moved the rules.

Kit. Drawn by ranked_bar(). Column module, 866 px; artboards 866, 560 and 328 px.

Studio note, not chart copy

S04 · Dot plot or dumbbell

Reader question. Which age groups vote, and did that change between two elections?

Why this form. Two dots per age group show the level and the change at once; printed values and the change in words carry the numbers without a grid.

Kit. Drawn by dumbbell(). Column module, 866 px; artboards 866, 560 and 328 px.

Studio note, not chart copy

S05 · Small multiples

Reader question. How far apart are homeownership rates by race, and has the gap closed?

Why this form. One panel per group on one scale lets a reader compare each group with the other three, which sit behind it in Stone.

Kit. Drawn by small_multiples(). Column module, 866 px; artboards 866, 560 and 328 px.

Studio note, not chart copy

S06 · Comparison table

Reader question. If a reform path were followed, which way would each outcome move?

Why this form. A table keeps the atlas's words in every cell; a glyph and a tint let a reader scan the up and down moves across eight rows without red or blue.

Kit. Drawn by comparison_table(). Column module, 866 px; one HTML table that reflows under 640 px.

Studio note, not chart copy

S07 · Map

Reader question. Where can a city adopt ranked-choice voting, and where has the state ruled it out?

Why this form. Equal tiles give every state the same weight and room for its code and the year of its ban; true shapes would hide the small eastern states.

Kit. Drawn by tile_map(). Column module, 866 px; artboards 866, 560 and 328 px.

Studio note, not chart copy

S08 · Unit chart

Reader question. Have the rules been moving toward voters or away from them?

Why this form. One square per record lets a reader count every change and find each one by number; two panels split at 2025 show when the changes away from voters came.

Kit. Drawn by unit_ledger(). Column module, 866 px; one HTML grid of 28 px units that stacks its two panels under 700 px.

Studio note, not chart copy

S09 · Timeline

Reader question. Which rule changes since 1870 decided who counts, who governs, who owns and who checks?

Why this form. Four lanes on one true time scale show when each thread changed; each dot carries its record key, and the list under the lane names every event in date order.

Kit. Drawn by timeline(). Column module, 866 px; artboards 866, 560 and 328 px.

Studio note, not chart copy

S10 · Evidence mix

Reader question. How much of each everyday answer rests on documented fact?

Why this form. A 100% bar per question compares the mix across questions of different sizes; sorting by the documented share puts the firmest answers first.

Kit. Drawn by evidence_mix(). Column module, 866 px; artboards 866, 560 and 328 px.

View 3 of 5 · Charcoal

Two modules on Charcoal

The dark palette swaps roles, not meanings: Newsprint carries the named series, Dim Newsprint the context, and texture still carries the evidence grade. Text from 13 to 15 px sets one weight heavier. Lifted Prussian and lifted Verdigris sit only 0.022 apart in lightness here, so dark charts keep to two inks and label every mark.

  • Named series and away from voters. Newsprint, #DCD9D2, 13.29:1
  • Context and secondary text. Dim Newsprint, #A3A19C, 7.26:1
  • Toward voters. Verdigris, 30% toward Newsprint, #76978F, 5.88:1
  • Middle level and quieter context. Stone, 35% toward Newsprint, #878A8F, 5.41:1
  • Well supported. Dim Newsprint, #A3A19C, 7.26:1
  • Gridline, decorative. Stone, 45% toward Charcoal, #393C41, 1.69:1
  • The headline's point. Pillar Red, #E63946, 4.49:1

View 4 of 5 · Social card

S01 as a 1080 by 1350 card

The card is the S01 module with its controls removed. big_number() draws a 524 px artboard and the card sets it at 1.82 times, so the smallest chart label reads at 24 px. The slots keep their order: evidence label, title, measure, figure, source. The wordmark comes from the display master, and the one red mark is the Senate shortfall the title names.

Studio note, not chart copy

Social card · built from S01

What changes. The switch, the downloads and the readout drop. The title, measure, figure, notes and source stay. The table travels as the alt text.

Size. 1080 by 1350 px, the portrait post for Instagram and LinkedIn; 64 px margins on the 8 px rhythm.

Kit. social_card(spec) measures the title, measure and source, then asks the generator for the narrowest artboard that fills the card's 952 px width and still fits the height left over. A module whose scale would fall under 1.6 times needs a shorter title or a shorter artboard.

View 5 of 5 · System

The kit on one sheet

What a builder needs to make the next chart without asking: the module's seven slots, its sizes, the type ramp, the marks, the codes, the palettes with measured contrast, the red rule, the annotation and source rules, and what changes between a still image and a panel.

01 The module

One chart, every part named. The letters in the margin match the table.

The seven slots
SlotHoldsTypeSpace above, px
A IndexEvidence label at left; the atlas record index at rightInter 700, 13/18, capitals, +0.06 em; index Inter 600, 13/18, tabular, Deep Stone2 px Charcoal rule, then 12
B TitleOne sentence that states the finding, its verb matched to the gradeInter Tight 800, 28/32, −0.025 em; 22/26 on phones8
C MeasureMeasure, unit, place and period; says where a scale starts if not at zeroInter 400, 15/22, Deep Stone8
D ControlsChart and Table switch at left, downloads at right. Panel onlyInter 600, 14; 32 px targets, 44 on phones16
E FigureOne artboard at 866, 560 or 328 px with its notes inside the drawing; or the tableLabels Inter 600, 13; notes Inter 400, 1316
F NotesCoding notes and qualifications a reader needs; the key only when labels cannot fitInter 400, 14/2016
G SourceSource line in section 15 order, credit at right; then a 1 px Stone ruleInter 400, 13/18, Deep Stone12, then 16 below

A slot never moves and never changes job. An empty slot closes up, except B, C, E and G, which every chart fills. The figure slot holds one artboard at a time: a container query picks 866 px when the module is that wide, 560 px from 560, and 328 px below, drawn to fill 328 to 358 px so labels never fall under 13 px.

02 Sizes and spacing

Widths

  • Column module, 866 px. 8 of 12 columns at 1440; the default for atlas pages and reports
  • Still, 680 px. Substack and email body; exported at 2x
  • Medium artboard, 560 px. Tablets and narrow windows
  • Social card artboard, 524 px. Chosen by social_card() and set at 1.82x to fill the 952 px content width of the 1080 by 1350 card
  • Phone artboard, 328 px. Drawn at 328, shown at 328 to 358 for 360 and 390 px phones

Spacing

Every gap is a step of the Signal Grid's 8 px rhythm, with its 4 px half step. Modules stack 72 px apart; slots sit 8 to 16 px apart; rows in a chart sit on 32 or 40 px.

Lora Italic sets quoted words inside a note and nothing else; no chart title or label uses a serif. On Charcoal, text from 13 to 15 px sets one weight heavier.

04 Marks

Line weights

  • 1 px. Hairline: gridlines in Stone 70% toward the ground, leaders, rules, the bar track
  • 1.5 px. Context lines in small multiples; the open ring for an earlier year; the pending outline
  • 2 px. Context series in a line chart; the 60-vote threshold; dumbbell connectors
  • 3 px. The series the title names, in Charcoal; the red point mark
  • 6 px. The lit selection in an interactive panel only

Marks

  • Units: 28 px squares on a 32 px pitch, numbered in Inter 600 13 px. Fill or outline carries the second code.
  • Ranked bars: 24 px tall on a 40 px pitch, a 16 px gap, counts inside when the segment is 18 px or wider. 100% bars: 18 px on a 32 px pitch.
  • Dots: 6 px radius for the later year, a 5 px open ring for the earlier; 5 px on a timeline; 4 px on a line where a note points.

05 Codes after color

Every code survives grayscale through a second channel: fill against outline, texture, shape or position.

Direction code, repair log

  • Away from voters. Charcoal fill. The named series when a title names it.
  • Toward voters. Verdigris strong fill: Verdigris 25% toward Charcoal in OKLab.
  • Kept existing rules. Stone light fill with a Stone outline.
  • Mixed. Split: both fills in one mark.
  • Pending. Open: a 1.5 px Charcoal outline on the ground, not yet decided.

Grayscale holds the order: Charcoal, Verdigris strong, Stone light, ground. Row position in S08 and segment order in S03 add a third code.

Evidence code

  • Documented. On the public record. Solid Charcoal.
  • Well supported. Strong research evidence. Solid gray, a step lighter.
  • Plausible. Some evidence. 2 px dashes, 8 on and 4 off, the atlas's plausible line.
  • Contested. Evidence disputed. Dash-dot at 8, 3, 2 and 3, the atlas's contested line.

Grades never take red, and hypothesis, the dotted line, has no fill: no claim in the register carries it.

Direction glyphs, scenarios

  • Up.
  • Slightly up.
  • Flat.
  • Flat or down.
  • Down.
  • Mixed.
  • Same as scenario ii.

Shape carries the direction; a Verdigris or Prussian tint carries the side, never red against blue. Party marks take neutral inks with the party's name printed on them, ordered by value or alphabet.

Contrast is WCAG 2 against the ground, computed by the build script. Every tint is one of the palette lab's OKLab mixes of locked colors; the build script recovered each mix and prints it above. identity colors never change. Kept existing rules, the up and down tints and the gridline fall under 3:1 by design: each kept segment prints its count and carries a Stone outline, each tinted cell prints the atlas's words, and gridlines carry no meaning. Verdigris and Stone sit 0.05 apart in lightness, so no chart separates two categories by those two inks alone. Pillar Red appears in the table as a swatch, which Rule 05.3 does not count.

07 Red

The wordmark's ampersand and the lockmark's lever are signature red and do not count, and neither do the ampersands inside the hinge diagram and the hinge-circle badge, which are identity marks. The hinge diagram never shares a view with the wordmark and never stands in for the hinge divider. An icon's red accent counts as signature red when the icon stands alone, as an app tile, an avatar or a single feature icon. In a row or a menu, icons go one color and only the current one keeps its red. Each view (one screen, card, slide or printed page) then carries one working red, in this order of precedence: an error the reader must fix; the step a reader can take now; the one point the headline names, which in a systems figure is where a reform acts. One job may take several marks, such as each target of one reform. A hinge headline's ampersand uses the view's working red. The hinge divider's ampersand takes its surface's ink: Charcoal on Newsprint and White, Newsprint on Charcoal, White on Prussian. In the guide itself, specimens, labeled failure cases and palette swatches do not count. Red never sits on Prussian.

Rule 05.3, the red rule (D2-01)

On a chart page each module counts as one view. Red never codes a series, a category, a scale, a party or a grade. It may mark the one point a title names, here the 7 votes the Senate fell short in S01, and only when no error or ask holds the view. Press the button to put an ask in this view: the ask takes the red, and the shortfall steps down to Charcoal at the same 3 px weight.

See how each senator votedIllustrative ask

08 Annotation and source lines

  1. Notes sit inside the drawing. Inter 13 in Deep Stone, joined to the data by 1 px leaders; the named record in Inter 600, Charcoal. A note names the record, explains an odd encoding once, or gives a reader's scale.
  2. Label directly. Labels sit on the mark or at its end. A key appears only when labels cannot fit, and it sits inside the drawing above the marks it explains.
  3. Write the unit once. On the top tick or the first label: "100%", "17 changes", "Down 3.7 points". Other ticks stay bare.
  4. Numbers are tabular, and minus is the true minus. −3.7, never a hyphen.
  5. Scales are honest. Bars start at zero. A line or dot scale may start elsewhere when the measure line says so. Small multiples share one scale. Missing years and method breaks stay open; the line never bridges them.
  6. Hover adds, never hides. The readout under a chart repeats what the table holds. Every value is printed, in the notes or in the table.
  7. The source line goes under every chart. In section 15 order: publisher, title or table, observation period, geography, date retrieved, qualification. Shorten by dropping words, never facts. The credit sits at the right.
  8. Index labels point at records. RL07 is repair log row 7, PW15 is everyday question 15, E09 is the studio's key for the ninth history event. They print where they help a reader find the record, and nowhere for decoration.
  9. Illustrative items carry the word. "Illustrative data" or "Illustrative ask" sits beside the item, never in a footnote.

09 Still image and interactive panel

Still and panel

  • Stays. Slots A, B, C, E, F and G in the same order and the same type; every printed number; every note; the source line.
  • Drops. Slot D: the Chart and Table switch and the downloads. The hover readout.
  • Adds. Alt text with every value, sent with the image, and a line in the notes that says where the table and data live.
  • Changes. The figure uses a 680 px artboard drawn by the same generator and exports at 2x for Substack and email. Nothing moves between slots.

This page offers CSV and SVG from the panel. A PNG still would come from an export step in the kit, which this concept does not build yet.

10 How to read our charts

For readers. This list can run on the atlas's help page and under a report's first chart.

  1. The small label above the title says what kind of claim the chart makes: a finding, an association, an estimate or an illustration.
  2. The title says what the chart found. The line under it names what was measured, where and when.
  3. The darkest mark is the one the title is about. Gray marks are there for comparison.
  4. A red mark, when a chart has one, points at the single thing the title names. It never stands for a party, a side or a group.
  5. Texture tells you how sure the atlas is. Solid means documented or well supported, dashes mean plausible, dash-dot means contested.
  6. Codes such as RL07 or PW15 are record numbers. Search the atlas for them to read the full record.
  7. Every chart has a Table button, and its source sits under it in both states. The downloads give you the same numbers.
